4:1.sourceText: Λέγω δέ, ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ὁ κληρονόμος νήπιός ἐστιν, οὐδὲν διαφέρει δούλου κύριος πάντων ὤν,
4:1.targetText: And I say, now as much time as the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a servant, [though] being lord of all,

unmappedTarget.reason: English adds a discourse now before the temporal comparison; no separate Greek now adverb is written.
Bracketed English concessive connector supplied for the being-lord participial clause.

4:2.sourceText: ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐστὶν καὶ οἰκονόμους ἄχρι τῆς προθεσμίας τοῦ πατρός.
4:2.targetText: but is under tutors and stewards until the time appointed of the father,

4:3.sourceText: οὕτως καὶ ἡμεῖς, ὅτε ἦμεν νήπιοι, ὑπὸ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου ἤμεθα δεδουλωμένοι·
4:3.targetText: so we also, when we were children, were in servitude under the elements of the world,

4:4.sourceText: ὅτε δὲ ἦλθεν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου, ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν Υἱὸν αὐτοῦ, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός, γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον,
4:4.targetText: and when the fullness of time came, God sent forth His Son, come of a woman, come under law,

groups.note: The Greek becoming/born participle is rendered come of a woman. The shared coming-into-existence predicate is retained without a separate Greek coming verb. The second becoming participle likewise supplies the English come under law.

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.

4:5.sourceText: ἵνα τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον ἐξαγοράσῃ, ἵνα τὴν υἱοθεσίαν ἀπολάβωμεν.
4:5.targetText: that He may redeem those under law, that we may receive the adoption as sons;

groups.note: Greek υἱοθεσία is son-adoption; LSV makes that meaning explicit with adoption as sons. No separate Greek sons noun is invented in this phrase.

4:6.sourceText: Ὅτι δέ ἐστε υἱοί, ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ Πνεῦμα τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν, κρᾶζον Ἀββᾶ ὁ Πατήρ.
4:6.targetText: and because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of His Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.
The Greek article occurs with the Father address; English uses the bare vocative Father.
Source-witness person difference: N1904 has ἡμῶν, our hearts, while LSV follows second-person your hearts.

unmappedTarget.reason: Source-witness person difference: the LSV second-person possessor differs from N1904 first-person ἡμῶν, our.

4:7.sourceText: ὥστε οὐκέτι εἶ δοῦλος ἀλλὰ υἱός· εἰ δὲ υἱός, καὶ κληρονόμος διὰ Θεοῦ.
4:7.targetText: So that you are no longer a servant, but a son, and if a son, also an heir of God through Christ.

groups.note: The actual God name is shared, but its relation changes: N1904 through God, LSV heir of God through Christ. The name alone remains linked; the unlike relationship wording is explained separately.

unmappedSource.reason: Source-witness relationship difference: N1904 has διὰ Θεοῦ, through God. LSV makes God the heir’s possessor and adds a through-Christ relation; its through does not govern the same original participant.

unmappedTarget.reason: English makes God the possessor of the inheritance; in N1904 the God genitive is governed by through, not an heir-of-God construction.
Source-witness difference: LSV follows the longer through-Christ wording, while N1904 writes through God without a Christ name here.

4:8.sourceText: Ἀλλὰ τότε μὲν οὐκ εἰδότες Θεὸν ἐδουλεύσατε τοῖς φύσει μὴ οὖσιν θεοῖς·
4:8.targetText: But then, indeed, having not known God, you were in servitude to those [that are] not by nature gods,

groups.note: Greek οὖσιν is the actual being participle. It supports the bracketed English that are; the brackets do not make the written Greek be predicate absent.

4:9.sourceText: νῦν δὲ γνόντες Θεόν, μᾶλλον δὲ γνωσθέντες ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα, οἷς πάλιν ἄνωθεν δουλεῦσαι θέλετε;
4:9.targetText: and now, having known God—and rather being known by God—how [do] you turn again to the weak and poor elements to which you desire anew to be in servitude?

groups.note: The actual finite second-person turning verb supplies the English question auxiliary do together with you turn. The English brackets do not make this real verbal counterpart absent.
The two Greek adverbs πάλιν ἄνωθεν express again from the beginning; the one English anew condenses their combined restart meaning, retaining both actual original identities.

4:10.sourceText: ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖσθε καὶ μῆνας καὶ καιροὺς καὶ ἐνιαυτούς.
4:10.targetText: You observe days, and months, and times, and years!

4:11.sourceText: φοβοῦμαι ὑμᾶς μή πως εἰκῇ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς.
4:11.targetText: I am afraid for you, lest I labored in vain for you.

4:12.sourceText: Γίνεσθε ὡς ἐγώ, ὅτι κἀγὼ ὡς ὑμεῖς, ἀδελφοί, δέομαι ὑμῶν. οὐδέν με ἠδικήσατε·
4:12.targetText: I implore you, brothers, become as I [am]—because I also [am] as you; you did not hurt me;

groups.note: The Greek adverbial nothing, οὐδέν, negates the injuring action; LSV expresses it as not without a separate in-anything complement.

unmappedTarget.reason: Bracketed English copula supplied after the first I.
Bracketed English copula supplied after I also.

4:13.sourceText: οἴδατε δὲ ὅτι δι’ ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν τὸ πρότερον,
4:13.targetText: and you have known that through weakness of the flesh I proclaimed good news to you at the first,

4:14.sourceText: καὶ τὸν πειρασμὸν ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου οὐκ ἐξουθενήσατε οὐδὲ ἐξεπτύσατε, ἀλλὰ ὡς ἄγγελον Θεοῦ ἐδέξασθέ με, ὡς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν.
4:14.targetText: and you did not despise nor reject my trial that [is] in my flesh, but you received me as a messenger of God—as Christ Jesus;

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.
Source-witness possessor difference: N1904 has ὑμῶν, your trial, while LSV has my trial. The actual first-person μου later in the verse modifies flesh and remains linked there.

unmappedTarget.reason: Source-witness possessor difference: LSV has my trial, where pinned N1904 writes second-person ὑμῶν, your.
English supplies a relative connector to express the Greek trial-in-my-flesh prepositional modifier.
Bracketed English copula supplied in that modifier.

4:15.sourceText: ποῦ οὖν ὁ μακαρισμὸς ὑμῶν; μαρτυρῶ γὰρ ὑμῖν ὅτι εἰ δυνατὸν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑμῶν ἐξορύξαντες ἐδώκατέ μοι.
4:15.targetText: what then was your blessedness? For I testify to you, that if possible, having plucked out your eyes, you would have given [them] to me;

groups.note: The written Greek eyes noun is the shared object of plucking out and giving. LSV resumes those same eyes with bracketed them after given; both English mentions retain the actual eyes identity, without inventing a Greek personal pronoun.
The Greek aorist giving predicate occurs in the elided if-possible condition; LSV makes its unreal-result sense explicit with you would have given, without an independently written Greek modal verb.

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.
Source-witness interrogative difference: N1904 has ποῦ, where, while LSV gives what, following a different interrogative reading.

unmappedTarget.reason: Source-witness interrogative difference: LSV asks what, while pinned N1904 asks where with ποῦ.
English copula supplied in the initial blessedness question; no finite Greek copula is written there.

4:16.sourceText: ὥστε ἐχθρὸς ὑμῶν γέγονα ἀληθεύων ὑμῖν;
4:16.targetText: so have I become your enemy, being true to you?

4:17.sourceText: ζηλοῦσιν ὑμᾶς οὐ καλῶς, ἀλλὰ ἐκκλεῖσαι ὑμᾶς θέλουσιν, ἵνα αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦτε.
4:17.targetText: They are zealous for you—[yet] not well, but they wish to shut us out, that you may be zealous for them;

unmappedSource.reason: The displayed LSV has first-person us as the object of shutting out; N1904 explicitly has second-person ὑμᾶς, you. These different persons remain unpaired.

unmappedTarget.reason: The displayed first-person us differs from the second-person ὑμᾶς, you, written in pinned N1904.
Bracketed English contrast supplement; no separate corresponding Greek word is written.

4:18.sourceText: καλὸν δὲ ζηλοῦσθαι ἐν καλῷ πάντοτε, καὶ μὴ μόνον ἐν τῷ παρεῖναί με πρὸς ὑμᾶς,
4:18.targetText: and [it is] good to be zealously regarded, in what is good, at all times, and not only in my being present with you;

groups.note: The Greek substantival good adjective is rendered as the English relative what is good; the adjectival constituent supplies that whole nominal expression without a separate Greek what pronoun.

unmappedTarget.reason: Bracketed English subject and copula supplied in the initial nominal good statement.

4:19.sourceText: τέκνα μου, οὓς πάλιν ὠδίνω μέχρις οὗ μορφωθῇ Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν·
4:19.targetText: my little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ may be formed in you,

groups.note: The Greek accusative relative names the people metaphorically borne in travail; English uses of whom with its birth-travail predicate, retaining the same actual children.

unmappedTarget.reason: Source-witness diminutive difference: LSV follows the little-children form τεκνία; pinned N1904 has simple τέκνα, children.

4:20.sourceText: ἤθελον δὲ παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἄρτι καὶ ἀλλάξαι τὴν φωνήν μου, ὅτι ἀποροῦμαι ἐν ὑμῖν.
4:20.targetText: indeed I was wishing to be present with you now, and to change my voice, because I am in doubt about you.

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.

4:21.sourceText: Λέγετέ μοι, οἱ ὑπὸ νόμον θέλοντες εἶναι, τὸν νόμον οὐκ ἀκούετε;
4:21.targetText: Tell me, you who are willing to be under law, do you not hear the Law?

4:22.sourceText: γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι Ἀβραὰμ δύο υἱοὺς ἔσχεν, ἕνα ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης καὶ ἕνα ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας.
4:22.targetText: For it has been written that Abraham had two sons, one by the maidservant and one by the free [woman],

groups.note: The feminine substantival free adjective identifies the free woman; LSV makes that person explicit with bracketed woman. No separate Greek woman noun is invented.

4:23.sourceText: ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης κατὰ σάρκα γεγέννηται, ὁ δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας διὰ τῆς ἐπαγγελίας.
4:23.targetText: but he who [is] of the maidservant has been according to flesh, but he who [is] of the free [woman], through the promise,

groups.note: The substantival feminine free adjective identifies the free woman; its bracketed English woman makes that person referent explicit without a separate Greek woman noun.

unmappedSource.reason: Greek μέν marks the first side of the contrast; English uses the paired but clauses without a separate indeed.
N1904 explicitly writes the birth verb γεγέννηται, has been born. The displayed LSV prints has been but omits the birth lexical head; it is not falsely treated as a Greek copula.

unmappedTarget.reason: English prints only an auxiliary-like has been here; N1904 has the lexical birth predicate has been born, with no separate Greek copula. The missing birth head is explained rather than inventing an exact bare-be correspondence.
Bracketed English copula supplied in the first he-who-of-the-maidservant modifier.
Bracketed English copula supplied in the second he-who-of-the-free-woman modifier.

4:24.sourceText: ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα· αὗται γάρ εἰσιν δύο διαθῆκαι, μία μὲν ἀπὸ ὄρους Σινᾶ, εἰς δουλείαν γεννῶσα, ἥτις ἐστὶν Ἄγαρ,
4:24.targetText: which things are allegorized, for these are the two covenants: one, indeed, from Mount Sinai, bringing forth to servitude, which is Hagar;

4:25.sourceText: τὸ δὲ Ἄγαρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ· συνστοιχεῖ δὲ τῇ νῦν Ἱερουσαλήμ, δουλεύει γὰρ μετὰ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς.
4:25.targetText: for this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and corresponds to the Jerusalem that now [is], and is in servitude with her children,

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.
Source-witness connective difference: N1904 has δέ at the opening, while LSV introduces this Hagar explanation with for.
N1904 introduces the servitude explanation with γάρ, for; LSV coordinates it with and rather than retaining the explanatory connective.

unmappedTarget.reason: LSV gives an explanatory for at the opening, unlike the δέ written in pinned N1904.
English supplies this before the Hagar name; the Greek has a neuter article with the name, not a written demonstrative.
English adds a relative connector before now; the Greek has the present-Jerusalem modifier without a separate relative pronoun.
Bracketed English copula supplied after now.
LSV coordinates the servitude clause with and, while pinned N1904 has explanatory γάρ there.

4:26.sourceText: ἡ δὲ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν, ἥτις ἐστὶν μήτηρ ἡμῶν·
4:26.targetText: and the Jerusalem above is the free [woman], which is mother of us all,

groups.note: Greek free is a feminine predicate adjective with Jerusalem; LSV nominalizes it as the free woman in the mother allegory. The whole free-person predicate is retained without inventing a separate Greek woman noun.

unmappedTarget.reason: Source-witness quantifier difference: LSV follows the additional πάντων with us; pinned N1904 has ἡμῶν without a separate all.

4:27.sourceText: γέγραπται γάρ Εὐφράνθητι, στεῖρα ἡ οὐ τίκτουσα, ῥῆξον καὶ βόησον, ἡ οὐκ ὠδίνουσα· ὅτι πολλὰ τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐρήμου μᾶλλον ἢ τῆς ἐχούσης τὸν ἄνδρα.
4:27.targetText: for it has been written: “Rejoice, O barren, who is not bearing; break forth and cry, you who are not travailing, because many [are] the children of the desolate—more than of her having the husband.”

unmappedTarget.reason: Bracketed English copula supplied in the many-children nominal statement.

4:28.sourceText: ὑμεῖς δέ, ἀδελφοί, κατὰ Ἰσαὰκ ἐπαγγελίας τέκνα ἐστέ.
4:28.targetText: And we, brothers, as Isaac, are children of promise,

groups.note: Greek ἐστέ is second-person plural are; the displayed English are has first-person we as subject. The shared be predicate is retained with its person difference explicit and the unlike pronouns left unpaired.

unmappedSource.reason: Source-witness person difference: N1904 explicitly has second-person ὑμεῖς, you, while LSV gives first-person we.

unmappedTarget.reason: Source-witness person difference: LSV uses we, while pinned N1904 writes you.

4:29.sourceText: ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ τότε ὁ κατὰ σάρκα γεννηθεὶς ἐδίωκεν τὸν κατὰ Πνεῦμα, οὕτως καὶ νῦν.
4:29.targetText: but as he then who was born according to the flesh persecuted him [born] according to the Spirit, so also now;

groups.note: The Greek birth participle is written once for the child born according to the flesh. LSV repeats born in brackets for the parallel Spirit-related predicate; both English mentions share this actual written birth identity rather than a second invented Greek word.

4:30.sourceText: ἀλλὰ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή; Ἔκβαλε τὴν παιδίσκην καὶ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῆς· οὐ γὰρ μὴ κληρονομήσει ὁ υἱὸς τῆς παιδίσκης μετὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἐλευθέρας.
4:30.targetText: but what does the Writing say? “Cast forth the maidservant and her son, for the son of the maidservant may not be heir with the son of the free [woman]”;

groups.note: The Greek future inheriting verb is rendered by the English predicate may be heir. The inheritance/heir relation belongs to that whole verb rendering, not to a separate Greek heir noun.

unmappedSource.reason: Greek article is not separately expressed in this English possessive, personal-name or noun construction.

4:31.sourceText: διό, ἀδελφοί, οὐκ ἐσμὲν παιδίσκης τέκνα ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐλευθέρας.
4:31.targetText: then, brothers, we are not a maidservant’s children, but the free [woman’s].

groups.note: The genitive feminine free adjective denotes the free woman; English expresses its possessive role as free woman’s, with woman bracketed. No separate Greek woman noun is invented.
